items.title: Inside the quiet reinvention of corporate learning
items.summary: Psychologist Pauline Boss coined the term “ambiguous loss” to describe a grief with no clear boundaries, like that experienced by families whose loved ones were missing in action and who could neither grieve nor move on. Since ChatGPT arrived in late 2022, I’ve seen a version of it every day in my work with people across companies. Nothing has been taken from us, and yet something has disappeared. Expertise works like territory. Being the person who can do a particular thing marks out our place, and who we are at work depends on holding on to it. So when AI produces the same output we do, it can feel like it’s crossing an invisible line and chipping away at that identity. Those of us who work in corporate learning, or learning and development (L&D), have long been identified with content production: through training sessions and e-learning courses, we were responsible for gathering information and sharing it throughout the company. Whether any of it changed how people worked was hardly ever how we measured success. But now AI tools can bottle knowledge and deliver it at the right moment, in the form people need it, freeing L&D teams to do something else. What that something else should be is rarely discussed, and this silence is what makes the loss so ambiguous. This article is a book excerpt from L&D Rewired, How L&D Professionals Are Breaking Their Own Rules To Stay Relevant , by Lavinia Mehedintu For years, L&D has identified with what it does: with the training and workshops it provides, but fewer have been able to see its purpose in what it delivers: more effective people and organizations. I think this is what has caused a lot of the dread in our profession. The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 puts systems thinking among the skills that are likely to be in greatest demand through 2030. Systems thinking is the ability to see how the parts of an organization connect and influence each other. For L&D people, this means looking beyond the request for a course to the conditions that prevent performance. It is the difference between treating a symptom and getting to the root cause. A few years ago, the CEO of a global technology company asked the People & Culture leaders of his organization to teach employees and managers about the concept of accountability. Teams kept making commitments they didn’t keep, so he wanted everyone to be reminded of what accountability means. The team could have built the workshop and rolled it out globally. Yet, they had a hunch there was more to the story. So, instead, they spent a few weeks interviewing leaders across R&D, operations, finance, legal, and commercial, asking where the gaps actually were and what would genuinely help. What they learned was that some functions already had strong accountability, built on clear revenue targets and weekly rituals around shared dashboards. Even so, gaps did exist and they looked different in each place. In one function, responsibilities had not been defined clearly after a reorganization, so people were uncertain of what they were responsible for. In a third, the handovers between departments had no standard procedures, so when a piece of work fell apart, there was no one to turn to. The leaders hardly ever said that the problem lay in people not understanding what accountability meant. What they wanted was clarity on what was expected of them, and help with managing people who were failing to do their jobs properly. When asked if they needed training for their managers, most said they did not. The team went back to the CEO with a plan that looked nothing like the one he’d asked for: goal-setting built into the performance cycle, clearer OKRs at senior level, shared metrics for cross-functional teams, recognition tied to results, and an explicit conversation with the leadership team about role modeling. Learning was one piece of that plan, but accountability would only increase if several conditions were in place at once. What this L&D team did was simple, but not easy. Instead of delivering the training as requested, they stepped back and asked, “What is driving this problem?” That takes courage. It goes against what most stakeholders expect from L&D, and the answer often points to solutions that sit far outside a learning team’s usual scope. Looking at a problem systemically might reveal a need for clearer expectations, more timely feedback, or stronger processes and measures. It might also reveal that people need a space to meet, disagree, and align. Used well, systemic thinking turns L&D into a source of clarity for the whole organization, helping leaders and teams ask deeper questions and frame their problems better. The solutions that follow, however, rarely require content design. For many L&D teams, this is where the uncertainty starts. They can see the problem more clearly than ever, but they’re not sure what their part in solving it should be. The answers I see most often are small departures from what L&D has always done, seeds of what the field could become. Some teams are using facilitation to help leaders align and make decisions. Others use experience design to make learning memorable, and behavioral science to help people turn what they learn into long-term habits. Each one shifts L&D’s role from producing content toward changing how people and organizations work. In the end, perhaps, the future of corporate learning is not about learning at all, at least not in the way we know it. What we’re losing is a way of doing our work which no longer serves a purpose. What we are gaining is the part that AI can’t do, the chance to help people and organizations change, not just learn. This article is a book excerpt from L&D Rewired, How L&D Professionals Are Breaking Their Own Rules To Stay Relevant , by Lavinia Mehedintu. The book is about the identity challenge L&D professionals are currently going through. Each chapter explores a discipline (systems thinking, experience design, behavioral science, facilitation, and AI) through theory, research, tools, and real-world examples. You can purchase the book here . This article Inside the quiet reinvention of corporate learning is featured on Big Think .

items.title: What makes something real?
items.summary: What is the color red? What counts as a mountain versus a hill? What is a president, and what powers does a president have? According to Lisa Feldman Barrett, PhD, a University Distinguished Professor of Psychology at Northeastern University, the answers have something important in common: They depend, at least in part, on people collectively assigning meaning to physical signals in the world. “What you do, what you don’t do, what you say, what you don’t say — your daily actions help to constitute reality, help to manifest reality,” Barrett says. A different way to think about reality It’s part of a theory known as “relational realism,” which holds that many features we assume are objective aspects of reality actually emerge from the relationships between what exists in the world and what exists within us. Take color. Red isn’t simply a property of an object. It’s a property of the relationship between the wavelengths of light that hit your retina and the signals processed in your brain. How does your brain know to interpret those signals as red? You had to learn what those patterns meant, which means, at some point, other people helped teach you. How your Perception Box is built Barrett refers to this process of learning to assign meaning to physical signals as “cultural inheritance.” “Cultural inheritance is how other people, by virtue of their actions and their words, wire your brain with the remembered past that you now use to create the relational present,” she says. “Cultural inheritance is a form of passing knowledge from one generation to another.” In other words, much of the knowledge and meaning we use to understand reality isn’t simply out there waiting for us to discover it. It’s also passed down by those around us, becoming part of our Perception Box: the invisible mental container of accumulated experiences and concepts we use to make sense of the world. The reality we create together When groups of people collectively assign meaning to something that doesn’t intrinsically carry that meaning on its own, they create what’s referred to as “social reality.” It depends on some degree of shared understanding or consensus. Consider a burgundy chair. The wavelengths of light reaching your eyes don’t come labeled “burgundy.” Rather, your identification of that color depends on patterns you learned in the past and now use to interpret the signals reaching your brain. “So, in all cases, the signals outside our heads are given meaning by their relation to the signals inside our heads by consensus — by collective agreement — which means that even something like the existence of color is a form of social reality,” Barrett explains. How collective agreement creates — or erases — value Money is a classic example of social reality. “Every time you trade little pieces of paper for something that you can eat or that you can use, you are not just agreeing to the existence of money, you are manifesting the existence of money,” Barrett says. “And the more people who agree, the more solidified the value becomes.” Thus, if enough people were to withdraw their shared agreement that those pieces of paper could be exchanged for goods, that form of money would lose the meaning that gives it economic power. Barrett points to the 2008 mortgage crisis as an example of what happens when collective judgments about value shift dramatically, describing it as a moment “where a group of guys in suits withdrew their consent that mortgages had a certain value.” In other words, social realities can crumble, with real consequences, Barrett says: “The world was plunged into an economic crisis as a result.” Reality can bend, but only so far While reality is perspective-dependent and flexible, it’s not infinitely flexible. “You can’t just make up any bullshit, get consensus for it, and then it counts as true,” she says. “We could get a bunch of people to agree that [crushed] glass is food, but that would not make it true.” Barrett explains that’s because shared meaning is never the only signal that matters; in the example above, there are biological constraints helping to determine what counts as food. “The patterns that emerge from those signals also matter a great deal. They’re crucial.” In the end, we are all contributing to reality by what we do and don’t do. Whether we vote or don’t vote, follow a social influencer or don’t, or choose to eat one thing instead of another — all of those decisions manifest the reality we have to deal with. “You have more power for which signal patterns count as reality and which ones do not,” Barrett says. We interviewed Lisa Feldman Barrett for Relational Realism , a Big Think interview series created in partnership with Unlikely Collaborators . As a creative non-profit organization, they’re on a mission to help people challenge their perceptions and expand their thinking. Often that growth can start with just a single unlikely question that makes you rethink your convictions and adjust your vantage point. Watch the third episode above, and visit Perception Box to see more in this series. This video What makes something real? is featured on Big Think .

items.title: The Time is Right for a ‘Great Books’ Revival
items.summary: In 1970, the poet, educator, and architect June Jordan posed the following question during a middle-school graduation speech in Ocean Hill, Brooklyn: “Where are the central, required courses that will teach us our real heritage of heroes and heroines, rebellion, and loving accomplishment?” Questions like this are at the forefront of my mind lately. Like Jordan, I’m a writer who teaches students of all ages. As a literature professor at MIT , I’m working to develop Great Books programming—inspired by her dream of what a general curriculum might look like—that centers the history, poetics, and philosophy of science. Toward that end, I spent the past summer talking to physicists, poets, political scientists, materials-science engineers, and high-school teachers in English and robotics about the literary works that shaped their lives. You’ll recognize some of the authors whose names emerged from those conversations. Homer , Hansberry, Virgil, Whitman , Dickinson, and Dewey all made appearances. So did Melville and Morrison , Douglass and Du Bois . The central theme of our list was invention —the dance between the examined life and the art of self-creation. A number of these colleagues and friends are now working with me to build a program that will live at MIT but also be available to the general public: a set of living documents and dynamic conversations, open access, available to all. What we are trying to do is not just help ground students—the large majority of them scientists and engineers in training—in a humanistic research program, but to identify irreplaceable ideas during a time of accelerated change. In the world beyond campus, each day brings news about the dangers and wonders of artificial intelligence: that it will lead to economic abundance, the end of a range of life-threatening diseases, and the light-speed distribution of human knowledge around the globe. At the same time, reports warn of declining rates of literacy and damage to our working memories, the potential for mass job loss, and possibly much worse. Why many people have stopped reading, or no longer see the beauty or necessity of it, is one matter. But the question of why reading—especially reading that challenges and surprises us—is presently indispensable is another. How might timeless works of art, literary and otherwise, help prepare each of us for this new world? Every educational reform has to meet its particular moment. And the cultural turn toward artificial intelligence is only part of what makes this project timely: In my view, we need a renewed emphasis not just on the arts and humanities as such, but on making meaningful connections between humanistic thinking and technological development. We need to clarify, often and in public, why the pursuit of scientific knowledge matters in the first place, as well as what we actually want pathbreaking new technologies to offer us. Just as important, we must equip young people with the tools they need to navigate a social and political landscape that is growing more hostile toward the core premises of higher learning and scientific research. My sense of the transformative power of literature didn’t come from the academy. It is an inheritance, largely from my great-grandmother. She was born 30 years after the abolition of slavery, lived into the 1980s, and ultimately shaped my mother’s approach to education. The beauty of reading, she told her, of what you learn and preserve in your mind, is that it can never be stolen. It is yours the way little else in this life is yours. A reader is never entirely alone; the text opens a portal between friends and strangers, the dead and the living. Amid a nationwide crisis in education—and a parallel crisis of transcendent meaning and social belonging—my sense is that this is a crucial time to return to works that help us practice patience, astonishment, and deep attention to the details of the world around us. This work, if it is effective, will not only beautify our days. It will also make us more courageous, imaginative, and free. There has never been broad agreement on exactly what constitutes a core curriculum. Its history in the United States is marked by a series of debates that continue into the present. The “ Yale Report of 1828 ” reflects this reality: After describing the foundation of a “thorough education” for college students, the document identifies the “two great points to be gained in intellectual culture” as “the discipline and the furniture of the mind.” For its authors, the imagination of a young person was akin to a physical space that demanded a particular kind of structure, and adornment. [ Read: Stop meeting students where they are ] This report is conscious, from its first pages, of the new possibilities offered by science education; one early passage describes visiting Yale alumni who “express their surprise” at the fact that, since they’ve graduated from an institution once primarily devoted to religious education, “whole sciences have, for the first time, been introduced.” Anticipating the criticisms their version of the core curriculum may face, the authors pose a rhetorical question: “But why, it may be asked, should a student waste his time upon studies that have no immediate connection with his future profession?” Their answer, like the query itself, seems prescient today: “Every thing throws light upon everything.” Little more than a century later, another Great Books curriculum, at St. John’s College, likewise incorporated the sciences into its sprawling vision: Its four-year reading list included “classic works in philosophy, literature, political science, psychology, history, religion, economics, math, chemistry, physics, biology, astronomy, music, language, and more.” Columbia University has had a core curriculum since 1919. Wanting to know why it continues to resonate with students today, I called a colleague, Roosevelt Montás . A Columbia alumnus, he directed its Center for the Core Curriculum for a decade. Last year, Montás became an endowed professor at Bard College, which has a first-year Great Books seminar; as part of his new position, he travels across the country speaking with other institutions about their visions of what a Great Books program should look like. Montás has an expansive sense of the promise and power of a core curriculum, incorporating widely accepted classics—by Milton, Shelley, et al.—into a larger, universal syllabus, a gathering of ancient and contemporary authors who enhance our understanding of what it means to be human across time and space. When we spoke, Montás interwove the story of his life into this larger vision: Arriving in New York from the Dominican Republic at 12 years old; learning English alongside other first-generation students in Queens; choosing Columbia because it was “the most selective school that I could get to on the subway.” Once there, Montás was immediately struck by the creative resources that the Columbia Core offered him. The program is grounded primarily in foundational texts from around the world that are studied across two years. The first year focuses on epic poetry, fiction, religious literature, and drama: from the Epic of Gilgamesh to The Aeneid , and on through the King James Bible, Dante and Shakespeare, Austen and Woolf. The second year explores philosophy and politics, beginning with Plato and concluding with the works of Frantz Fanon, Simone de Beauvoir, and others. While pursuing his Ph.D. at Columbia, Montás went on to teach these classes to a new generation of students who, like him, sought not just historical knowledge, or higher meaning, but common ground. The set of programs we are working to establish at MIT—ones that bridge the sciences and the humanities and reach beyond campus—has its precedents. items.title: I Might Sleep With My Neighbor, If She Isn’t My Half-Sister
items.summary: An excerpt from This Vital Absence by Sophia Veltfort Every few weeks, Dean posted a new video about famous musicians he’d known in his prime. Eric Clapton, Frank Zappa, Pink Floyd. He sat in a black mesh chair in what looked like a home office. Behind him, shelves painted a fading cerulean held slender statuettes of birds with long necks and legs, their plumes carved in porcelain or bronze. He wore thin gray T-shirts, sometimes maroon, often a hoodie or crewneck sweatshirt, his receding gray hair pulled back in a ponytail. When he talked, his spine pitched him forward, his eyebrows shot up and down, and his voice lurched with emphasis. His desire for appreciation was so naked it embarrassed me, made me reassess my own prowess in camouflaging a desire that I harbored, too. Below one of his videos, someone had commented, This man is an idiot. He’d lost his medical license for administering anesthesia while high on fentanyl. He lived in upstate New York, he had my chin and eyelids, and he allegedly bore some responsibility in the death of a famous pop star. It was the summer of 2014, and I had just moved back to New York from a postgrad fellowship in the UK when my moms, Celeste and Lucia, emailed me what I would come to think of as the Dean Dossier. They’d done some sleuthing, they explained. I tried to follow their lines of inquiry through the clues they’d assembled, but there was no clear order to the documents they’d attached: a series of screenshots from a 2009 CNN interview; another of an acknowledgments section in Google Books, with a nurse’s name highlighted in yellow; a handful of news articles from the late 1980s and early nineties they’d downloaded or copy-and-pasted into RTFs (“New York, in Move to Bar AIDS, Puts New Limits on Sperm Banks,” October 4, 1989); local news items identifying the anesthesiologist on the pop star’s 1997 World Tour. They attached emails they’d exchanged with their fertility doctor following his release from prison in 2006 for insurance fraud, then a scan of a hand-drawn sketch I knew already of a man in profile who looked, it was true, much like the man in the screenshots. I got the gist of my moms’ missive. They thought they’d found something I wanted very much: my father’s name. Dean Nagler came up immediately in a Google search. Despite the bad press, he was no recluse. Stripped of his medical license, he’d started volunteering in a local bird sanctuary, and he spent his free time reminiscing about his heyday administering medicine to the stars. I respond to most messages within two hours , his Facebook page read. Of the hundreds of videos he’d posted, I picked a first one at random: a seven-minute and thirty-nine second discourse on The Who. For years I’d looked at men’s faces and seen my own in their features. I’d stand in line for the bus and think yes, from that forehead, from those hooded eyes, you could get mine. There had been an embarrassing incident in a subway station I tried not to think about, when I discovered that an older man’s attention did not necessarily mean a shared inference of genetic relation. But Dean looked just like me. I didn’t have to look for my features in his; they were right there. That night, there was a housewarming party that my roommate—Tom, an economist who’d been on the postgrad scholarship the same year as me—and I were planning to go to together. While I blow-dried my hair in our overlit bathroom, I glanced through the articles my moms had sent. Dean was a fuck-up, a real piece of work. I pictured him operating high, no one catching him, and tried to guess how it must have felt, that rush of perceived invincibility, of feeling golden, untouchable. I did know that feeling. It was the electric current running like a third rail beneath daily life. So often I’d tried to convince my parents and teachers I was reliable and good, but always it had felt like an optical illusion, a hologram through which shimmied the abyss. It was a relief to know I came from dissolution and recklessness. Dear Dean , I typed in a new Facebook message before I could hesitate. My mother was a patient of Dr. Nielson in 1989. I’m hoping to find the sperm donor. I wondered whether you might be willing to tell me if you ever donated sperm. Sincerely, Sylvia F. Tom was already putting on his shoes when I got to the living room. I still thought of him as the economist, though in the few weeks we’d lived together, it had become clear that he hadn’t studied economics, as such, but rather something to do with Marxist influences on the American administrative state during the New Deal period. He worked at McKinsey. I had a mostly virtual tutoring gig through a test prep company and vague plans to apply for more school and funded time to read and write. We weren’t crazy about each other but had both needed a place to live and had accepted an amicability, if not a friendship, as mutually beneficial. It was nice to have someone with whom to go places and come back at night. Tell me your secrets, he’d say, wagging his fingers like a conjuring magician as we stumbled up Broadway. Sometimes he’d recite the opening lines of The Canterbury Tales or Ecclesiastes. He tended to wear all denim and walk like he planned to be a senator, but he made me laugh when he flirted with me. The housewarming party was on 95th and Fifth Avenue, right by the brick armory that housed my old high school. The host, a mutual friend from Tom’s and my scholarship class, had recently inherited the apartment from his grandmother. Tom called the elevator. When it arrived, the car we stepped into was snug, almost too intimate. Beside me Tom seemed to feel this, too. He nudged his shoe against mine. Around the third floor, my phone vibrated in my pocket. Dean had written back. Holding my phone close, like a hand of cards I didn’t want Tom to see, I read, Hi, Sylvia, Nice to hear from you. I did indeed work with Dr. Nielson, but I never donated sperm. I hope you find what you’re looking for! When I looked up, I could just make out the shape of Tom’s eyes behind the lenses of his glasses still dark from outside. Tough day? he asked. My dad reached out to me, I said. Tom’s eyebrows rose above the flat top of his frames. I thought you didn’t have one. I didn’t, I said, but it’s him all right. Fuck, he said. What’s he like? I shrugged. A lot like everyone else: mostly pathetic with some redeeming comic features. You don’t think that, Tom said. The elevator doors pinged open. We headed through a marble foyer and into the party. At this point in a given outing, one of us usually glimpsed people we liked better and swiftly abandoned the other, but this time we made it to the drinks counter without either of our peeling off. Tom poured us each a shot of tequila and handed me a beer. Over the last couple of years, I’d noticed that people talked to me more when I slipped into an easy, thoughtless nihilism, and I loved this, as though I’d discovered how to morph into an electronegative oxygen molecule hogging electrons from the measly hydrogen I’d been most of my life. It was the changeability I liked, the sense that I had it in me to be many people. And it was easy, like going through the drawers under my childhood bed, finding an old treasure box I’d once carefully protected, realizing it held nothing I needed to keep. Tom returned his empty shot glass to the counter and considered me briefly. This the dad from your daddy issues essay? he asked. During orientation a couple of years ago, someone had found an essay I’d published in college, a humorless obsession piece about my unknown father, and had sent it around to the other people on our scholarship. I hadn’t realized Tom had seen it. I started to say it wasn’t a daddy issues essay but decided that wasn’t so inapt a description. items.title: What Vera Rubin Observatory’s first new dwarf planet means
items.summary: Back in 2006, the International Astronomical Union controversially demoted Pluto . This composite image of Pluto and its largest moon, Charon, was based on photographs taken by the New Horizons mission as it flew by the Plutonian planetary system back in 2015. Charon’s appearance is vastly different from Pluto’s, but both bodies are shown with the correct relative size and albedo. The surface features on Pluto show evidence of recent changes, indicating that the next time we visit Pluto to image it at this level of precision, it may exhibit a remarkably different appearance. Credit : NASA, APL, SwRI As part of that process, they officially defined “ planet ” and “ dwarf planet ” for the first time. The scientific line between planetary (above) and non-planetary (below) status, for three potential definitions of an orbit-clearing phenomenon and a star equal to the mass of our Sun. This definition could be extended to every exoplanetary system we can imagine to determine whether a candidate body meets the criteria, as we’ve defined them, for being classified as a true planet or not. Credit : J-L. Margot, Astron. J., 2015 Dwarf planets all: orbit the Sun, aren’t moons, achieve hydrostatic equilibrium, but don’t clear their orbits. The four largest asteroids, all shown here, have been imaged with NASA’s Dawn mission and the ESO’s SPHERE instrument. Ceres, the largest asteroid, is the smallest known body definitively in hydrostatic equilibrium. Vesta and Pallas are not, but Hygeia, with a smaller mass but a much lower density, may yet be; its status is indeterminate. Credit : NASA/JPL-Caltech/UCLA/MPS/DLR/IDA; ESO Therefore, sufficiently massive asteroids like Ceres , Under a size cutoff of 10,000 kilometers, objects within our solar system appear to be round, pulled into hydrostatic equilibrium via their gravity and rotation, combined. However, once you go to planetary radii below ~800 kilometers, hydrostatic equilibrium, or even roundness, are no longer certainties, but composition dependent. There are over 100 objects in hydrostatic equilibrium in our solar system, including asteroids, moons, planets, dwarf planets, and Kuiper belt and Oort cloud objects, but only 5 official dwarf planets as of 2026. Credit : Emily Lakdawalla; data from NASA/JPL, JHUAPL/SwRI, SSI, and UCLA/MPS/DLR/IDA Kuiper belt objects like Pluto , Eris , Makemake , and Haumea , The inner Solar System, including the planets, asteroids, gas giants, Kuiper belt, and more, is minuscule in scale when compared to the extent of the Oort cloud. Sedna, the only large object with a very distant aphelion, may be part of the innermost portion of the inner Oort cloud, but even that is disputed. On a linear scale, depicting the entire Solar System in a single image is incredibly limiting; to characterize the orbit of a faraway bound object requires years or even centuries of data. Credit : NASA/JPL-Caltech/R. Hurt and Oort cloud objects can achieve dwarf planethood. This chart shows the measured pressures (or constraints on pressure) around a variety of trans-Neptunian objects. Of all the objects ever measured through stellar occultations, only Pluto and 2002 XV93 were found to actually have non-zero atmospheres, with all other plutinos, including plutinos much larger than 2002 XV93, exhibiting no signature of an atmosphere at all. Credit : Ko Arimatsu et al., Nature Astronomy, 2026 Trans-Neptunian objects, ice-rich in composition, require estimated diameters of 400 km to likely achieve hydrostatic equilibrium . This image shows the Vera C. Rubin Observatory atop Cerro Pachón in Chile, with fairly typical cloud-free conditions accompanying it. When complete, Rubin Observatory will use its 8.4-meter telescope and 3200-megapixel camera to conduct an unprecedented, multi-color, decade-long survey of the optical sky called the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). The camera will be the largest ever constructed for astronomy, weighing an incredible 2.8 tonnes. Credit : Rubin Observatory/NSF/AURA Currently, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory surveys the visible southern skies every 3-4 nights. This image, taken in April of 2025, shows the completed and operational Vera C. Rubin Observatory with its dome open during its First Look observation activities. Overhead, the Beehive Cluster (Messier 41) shines bright, while below, the glow of nearby small cities shines in this mountainous landscape. Credit : RubinObs/NOIRLab/SLAC/NSF/DOE/AURA/P. Horálek (Institute of Physics in Opava) Through successive imagery, it uncovers faint, distant, migrating Solar System objects . This selection of 10 independent images of the same object, 2026 ED138, shows its migration relative to the backdrop of stars in the galactic plane. Only with Vera C. Rubin’s unique sensitivity and cadence can we discover objects this faint and distant in such a crowded field of view. Credit : NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA; Processing: M. Jurić (UW), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Helped by automated code, Rubin scientists identified the remarkable object 2026 ED 138 . “ Precovery ” images were spotted going back 10 years, enabling an orbital determination. This image shows the orbital pathway of newly discovered candidate dwarf planet 2026 ED138, as observed by the NSF’s Vera C. Rubin Observatory. The position at the start of each month between March and July of 2026 is highlighted with annotations. The orbital path is easily reconstructible based on the observed motion and rate of progression of the object across the sky, allowing us to determine its distance and status as a classical TNO. Credit : NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA; Acknowledgement: M. Jurić (UW), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Based on its distance, brightness, and estimated reflectivity, it’s definitely a Trans-Neptunian object . This top-down view of the Solar System shows the first five officially recognized dwarf planets, Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Makemake, and Haumea, along with the newest dwarf planet candidate: 2026 ED138. Observationally, 2026 ED138 is the 14th brightest TNO to date, but its physical size dimensions possess great uncertainties. Credit : NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R. Proctor; Processing: M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Its estimated size — between 600 km and 1500 km — places it firmly in dwarf planet territory . Over the course of just one month, the newly discovered candidate dwarf planet 2026 ED138 has migrated across this entire field of view of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Circled locations reveal instances where the telescope captured this Kuiper belt object migrating against the fixed background of stars. Credit : NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA; Processing: M. Jurić (UW), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) However, no new dwarf planets have been officially recognized by the IAU since 2006. This composite shows the 10 largest known Trans-Neptunian objects as of 2017, all classified as extremely likely to be dwarf planets. However, the IAU has officially recognized only 5 total worlds as dwarf planets as of 2026: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Makemake, and Haumea; the list has not been updated in over 20 years. Credit : Lexicon (Commons 3.0), Exoplanet Expert (Commons 4.0), SpaceDude777/Wikimedia Commons 2026 ED 138 , nicknamed “ Ed “, becomes the 103rd known Trans-Neptunian object 400+ km in diameter . The 14th brightest Trans-Neptunian object , future occultations should reveal its size. When one astronomical object occupies the same line-of-sight as another, an occultation will occur, as the “closer” object blocks the light that would otherwise be visible from the “farther” object. The Moon occults all of the other planets; the Moon and planets and other planetary bodies occult
